## 2026-09-30 - Step 1 - Gather requirements

Approved by the operator.

### requirements

### Purpose

Restarting the Engine API in place on one port takes the whole browser path down while the new process loads its FAISS index and warms up. That is tens of seconds on a full dataset (DEPLOYMENT.md §4, Triage "Engine `active` but `/api/health` refuses connections for minutes"). The browser path is nginx `:80` → Client backend `127.0.0.1:7072` → Engine `127.0.0.1:7070` (DEPLOYMENT.md §6; `client/backend/server.py` reads `--engine-url` once at startup, default `http://127.0.0.1:7070`). The build gives the operator one command that restarts the Engine on the code currently on disk (after a `git pull`, a dependency change or an environment change) with no window where the Client cannot reach an Engine. A second Engine starts on the other port of a fixed pair, is health-checked, and gets traffic through an nginx upstream switch; only then is the old one drained and stopped. Failures roll back on their own.

### Decided topology (operator decision)

- The Engine is what gets blue/green. The Client backend is not blue/green and is not restarted by a deploy.
- nginx is placed between the Client and the Engine through a new loopback-only listener on `127.0.0.1:7079`. It proxies every path to an nginx `upstream` whose single server is the active Engine port (`127.0.0.1:7070` or `127.0.0.1:7071`).
- The prod Client unit's `--engine-url` becomes `http://127.0.0.1:7079`, permanently. After this one-time change the Client never has to change or restart for an Engine deploy.
- The public `:80` site config (`/etc/nginx/sites-available/peertube-browser`, DEPLOYMENT.md §6) is not changed by this work. The `7079` listener must bind `127.0.0.1` only and must never be reachable from outside the host; the Engine has no authentication and `/internal/*` accepts writes (DEPLOYMENT.md §6 Firewall).

### Scope

- Prod contour only. The dev contour (`peertube-engine-dev` on 7171, Client dev on 7172) keeps its current single unit and in-place restart, unchanged.
- Fixed port pair `7070`/`7071` only: no free-port selection, no custom port list, no port options on the deploy script.
- Out of scope: fetching or updating code (the deploy restarts whatever is on disk), Client backend blue/green, dev-contour blue/green, unit hardening (review findings F1/F3), a per-request random-cache inode check, and `scripts/run-services.sh` (manual/dev runner without nginx; it keeps starting a single Engine on 7070).

### systemd instance template

- A template unit `peertube-engine@.service` replaces `peertube-engine.service` in the prod contour. The name follows the existing `peertube-engine` naming; the issue's `peertube-browser@.service` was only an example. The instance name is the port, so `peertube-engine@7070` and `peertube-engine@7071` can run at the same time.
- Template content matches today's prod Engine unit (`engine/install-engine-service.sh`): `Type=simple`, same `User=`, `WorkingDirectory=`, `Environment=PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1`, `Environment=ENGINE_INGEST_MODE=bridge`, `EnvironmentFile=-<project>/.env.bridge`, `Restart=on-failure`, `TimeoutStopSec=20`, `WantedBy=multi-user.target`. The one difference is that `ExecStart` takes `--port` from the instance name (`%i`), with `--host 127.0.0.1`.
- The prod Engine installer (`engine/install-engine-service.sh --mode prod`, also reached through `scripts/install-service.sh`) installs the template instead of the single unit. On an existing install it migrates: it stops and disables the old `peertube-engine.service`, removes its unit file, then starts and enables one instance, `peertube-engine@7070`, and writes the snippet pointing at 7070. Re-running the installer is idempotent; it must not flip or restart a healthy active instance just because it is re-run without `--force`.
- Exactly one instance is enabled for boot: the one the snippet names. A deploy enables the new instance and disables the old one.
- The Engine uninstaller (`engine/uninstall-engine-service.sh --mode prod`, and `scripts/uninstall-service.sh`) stops, disables and removes both instances and the template, and removes the nginx snippet and the 7079 listener config that the installer wrote. Afterwards nginx must still pass `nginx -t` and keep serving the public site.
- `--help` and `--dry-run` keep working on all installer and uninstaller entrypoints. `tests/run-installers-smoke.sh --dry-run-only` relies on both.

### nginx: single source snippet and internal listener

- One snippet file is the single source of truth for which Engine port is active. It contains only the upstream definition, one server line: `127.0.0.1:7070` or `127.0.0.1:7071`. Nothing else (no state file, no systemctl query) decides which port is active.
- A loopback-only server block listens on `127.0.0.1:7079`, includes or references that upstream, and proxies every path to it.
- The listener passes request headers through unchanged. In particular `X-Request-ID` from the Client must reach the Engine as sent: it is neither stripped nor replaced. `X-Client-IP` and `X-Bridge-Token` must also arrive unchanged, because the Engine's rate limiter keys on `X-Client-IP` (DEPLOYMENT.md §6) and `/internal/*` authenticates on `X-Bridge-Token` (§3b). This keeps the work compatible with `X-Request-ID` forwarding from issue `20-request-lifecycle-logs`, which is not delivered yet.
- Proxy timeouts on the listener must not cut off legitimate long Engine requests (up-next FAISS searches are not bounded by the 5 s statement deadline, DEPLOYMENT.md §4 "Up-next logs and load"). Keep nginx defaults or set them at least as generous.
- Setup of the snippet, the listener and the Client's `--engine-url` change is scripted, with no manual nginx edits: done by the prod install path (Engine and Client installers or the central `scripts/install-service.sh`). Setup validates with `nginx -t` before reloading.
- The prod Client installer (`client/install-client-service.sh --mode prod`) writes `--engine-url http://127.0.0.1:7079` by default. Dev keeps `http://127.0.0.1:7171`.

### Deploy command

- New script `scripts/deploy-bluegreen.sh`. It operates on the repository root the same way `scripts/run-services.sh` resolves it.
- It requires the explicit `--blue-green` flag. Without it the script prints usage and exits non-zero, with no side effects.
- It supports `--help` and `--dry-run`. Dry-run prints the detected active port, the target port, and every action it would take, without starting, stopping, writing or reloading anything.
- Options: a readiness timeout in seconds (default 300, matching `run-services.sh` `HEALTH_TIMEOUT`); an optional warm-up wait in seconds after the first healthy answer (default 0); a drain wait in seconds between the switch and stopping the old instance (default long enough for in-flight requests to finish; design picks the value and documents it).
- It runs as root (via sudo), like the installers, because it calls `systemctl` and `nginx`. It fails fast with a clear message otherwise, except in `--dry-run`.
- One command does the whole deploy. No step needs a manual `systemctl` call or nginx edit.

### Deploy flow

1. Acquire an exclusive non-blocking lock (flock on a fixed lock file). If another deploy holds it, exit non-zero at once with a message, touching nothing.
2. Refuse to start (non-zero, message) while the prod updater service (`peertube-updater.service`) is active, since it stops and starts the Engine itself.
3. Read the active port from the snippet. If the snippet is missing or names anything other than 7070/7071, stop with an error and touch nothing. The target port is the other one of the pair.
4. If the target instance is already running (leftover from an interrupted deploy), stop it first. A leftover is restarted, never reused, so the deploy always runs freshly started code.
5. Start `peertube-engine@<target>`.
6. Readiness: poll `http://127.0.0.1:<target>/api/health` until it returns HTTP 200 or the readiness timeout expires. The poll interval must stay well inside the Engine's `/api/` rate limit, because `/api/health` sits behind `_rate_limit_check`. Then wait the optional warm-up time and check health once more.
7. Switch: keep a copy of the current snippet, write the new snippet atomically (temp file plus rename) naming the target port, run `nginx -t`, then reload nginx.
8. Post-switch check: `http://127.0.0.1:7079/api/health` returns 200.
9. Wait the drain period, then stop `peertube-engine@<old>` with `systemctl stop` (SIGTERM; the Engine shuts down gracefully), enable the new instance and disable the old one.
10. Remove the old instance's leftover `engine/server/db/random-cache.tmp.<old MainPID>.db` if one exists. The PID is recorded before the stop. A stop during a background cache build leaves this file, and it is safe to delete (issue comment; DEPLOYMENT.md §4).
11. Release the lock and exit 0.

### Automatic rollback

- Readiness failure (timeout, or the target unit fails or exits): stop the new instance; the snippet and nginx are untouched and the old instance keeps serving. Exit non-zero.
- `nginx -t` failure, reload failure, or post-switch check failure: restore the previous snippet, run `nginx -t`, reload nginx, stop the new instance. The old instance keeps serving. Exit non-zero.
- The old instance is never stopped before the switch has been verified (step 8).
- After the switch is verified, failures (stopping the old instance, enable/disable, temp-file cleanup) are logged and make the exit code non-zero, but do not roll back the switch, because traffic is already on the new instance.
- A failure inside rollback itself (for example the restore's `nginx -t` fails) is logged loudly with the state left behind, and exits non-zero.
- The lock is released on every exit path, including signals.

### Idempotency

- Re-running after a successful deploy deploys again: it flips to the other port. Re-running after an interrupted or failed deploy converges, because the snippet is the only source of truth and a leftover target instance is restarted, not reused.
- A deploy never leaves both instances serving through nginx: the upstream names exactly one server at every moment.

### Updater compatibility

- `engine/server/db/jobs/updater-worker.py` currently stops and starts one fixed unit name (`--service-name`, default `peertube-engine`). In prod it must stop and start the active instance instead: the one the snippet names when the updater reaches its stop step. It must start the same instance it stopped.
- The updater's sudoers rule (`engine/install-updater-service.sh`, `/etc/sudoers.d/peertube-updater-systemctl`) must allow exactly `stop` and `start` on `peertube-engine@7070` and `peertube-engine@7071`, nothing broader.
- A deploy and the updater's Engine stop/start window must not overlap in either direction. The deploy refuses while the updater is active (flow step 2), and the updater must not stop/start an Engine while a deploy holds the lock; design picks the mechanism.
- Dev updater behaviour is unchanged.

### Random cache and similarity cache during the overlap

- Both instances building `random-cache.db` during the overlap (each with its own `random-cache.tmp.<pid>.db`) is accepted, as is the extra CPU while both run.
- Readiness does not wait for a random-cache build. `/api/health` does not report it, and the Engine serves the random feed from `whitelist.db` until its build finishes (DEPLOYMENT.md §4). The optional warm-up wait is the operator's control for this.
- No per-request inode check is added. Only one instance takes traffic at a time, and the old instance is stopped after the drain, so a sibling holding an old `random-cache.db` inode only lasts for the overlap.
- The similarity cache needs nothing new. Running Engines already reopen a swapped `similarity-cache.db` on their next cache access (DEPLOYMENT.md "The updater timer").

### Logging

- Every deploy has a deploy id, unique per run (for example UTC timestamp plus PID). Every log line carries it.
- Logged at minimum: deploy id, old port, new port, the switch time (when the reload succeeded), the health result (HTTP status and seconds waited, for readiness and for the post-switch check), the drain and stop outcome, and on any rollback the rollback reason and the step it happened at.
- Lines go to stdout and to journald through `logger` with a fixed tag, matching `log_lifecycle` in the installers (`logger -t peertube-service-lifecycle`, or a deploy-specific tag; design picks).

### Documentation

- Every other doc that names `peertube-engine.service` for prod, or 7070 as the only prod Engine port, is brought in line (`README.md`, `engine/server/README.md`, `engine/server/db/jobs/docs/UPDATER_WORKER.md`, as the impact inventory finds them).

They cover: a normal flip 7070→7071 and back 7071→7070 (snippet contents, start/stop/enable/disable calls in order, old stopped only after the switch); readiness-timeout rollback (new stopped, snippet unchanged, old untouched, non-zero exit); `nginx -t` failure rollback; reload failure rollback; post-switch probe failure rollback (previous snippet restored); lock contention (second run exits non-zero without side effects); refusal without `--blue-green`; refusal while the updater is active; leftover target instance restarted; missing or invalid snippet refused; leftover `random-cache.tmp.<old pid>.db` removed; required log fields present, including the rollback reason.
- The updater's active-instance resolution and the installer's template/sudoers output are covered by tests or by dry-run contract checks in `tests/run-installers-smoke.sh --dry-run-only`.
- Operator validation on the live host, not automated: repeated deploys show no 5xx spike in the nginx access log for the public site, and a forced failure (for example a readiness timeout of 1 s, or a deliberately broken snippet) exercises rollback with the old instance still serving.

Engine `--dev` default port vs green port: `engine/server/api/server.py` `DEV_SERVER_PORT = 7071` (and the `--dev` help text "bind port 7071") vs the requirement that `peertube-engine@7071` be the second prod instance. A manual `server.py --dev` run on the prod host takes the green port and makes the deploy's start of `@7071` fail its readiness check (that rolls back safely, but the deploy is blocked). The dev contour units are not affected, because they pass `--port 7171` explicitly.
Issue's example unit name `peertube-browser@.service` vs the existing naming `peertube-engine[-dev]` in `engine/install-engine-service.sh`, `engine/install-updater-service.sh` and `updater-worker.py`: the requirements use `peertube-engine@.service`, with operator approval.
Issue text "switch the nginx upstream" vs the tree: today nginx proxies only the Client backend on 7072 (DEPLOYMENT.md §6) and the Client reaches the Engine directly via a startup-fixed `--engine-url`. The operator resolved this by adding the loopback nginx listener on 7079 and pointing the prod Client at it.
`tests/check-frontend-client-gateway.sh` lists 7070/7071/7072/7171 as forbidden frontend API bases but not the new internal port 7079, so a frontend hardcoding `127.0.0.1:7079` would slip past that check.

## 2026-09-30 - Step 2 - Develop a solution

Approved by the operator.

### initial_solution

### Approach

The build has four parts. One bash script does the deploy. The Engine installer and uninstaller learn about the template unit and own the nginx files. The updater gets one extra argument for prod. The docs and tests are updated to match. Nothing in the Engine's Python server changes, and there are no new dependencies: the script uses only bash, `flock(1)` from util-linux, `curl`, `systemctl`, `nginx` and `logger`.

**nginx files (owned by the prod Engine installer).** There are two files.

- **The snippet**, `/etc/nginx/peertube-engine-upstream.conf`. It holds only `upstream peertube_engine { server 127.0.0.1:<port>; }` and is the single source of truth for the active port. It sits outside `conf.d/` so nothing else includes it by accident.
- **The listener**, `/etc/nginx/conf.d/peertube-engine-internal.conf`. It includes the snippet by absolute path and declares one `server` that listens on `127.0.0.1:7079` only, with `location /` doing a `proxy_pass` to `http://peertube_engine`.
  - **Headers pass through.** nginx forwards client request headers unchanged by default, so `X-Request-ID`, `X-Client-IP` and `X-Bridge-Token` reach the Engine as sent. The block sets no `proxy_set_header` for them. The only header line is `proxy_set_header Host $http_host`, so that `Host` is passed through too instead of being replaced with the upstream name.
  - **Timeouts and body size.** Proxy timeouts stay at the nginx defaults (60 s read/send). The Client's longest Engine timeout is 20 s (`ENGINE_PROXY_ROUTE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` for `/api/video/refresh`). `client_max_body_size` is set explicitly at or above the Client's `ENGINE_PROXY_MAX_BODY_BYTES` (1 000 000), so the new hop cannot add a 413.
  - **No upstream keepalive, on purpose.** Each request opens a new connection, so after a reload no connection stays pinned to the old port.
  - **Instance tag.** The listener adds a response header `X-Engine-Upstream: $upstream_addr`. The post-switch check uses it (see Risks). It is safe because the Client backend copies only `content-type` from Engine responses (`client/backend/server.py`), so the header never reaches a browser.
- **Why `conf.d`.** It is included in the `http` context by the stock Debian/Ubuntu `nginx.conf`, and `sites-available/peertube-browser` is not touched. After writing, the installer runs `nginx -t`, reloads, and then checks `127.0.0.1:7079/api/health`. If the host's `nginx.conf` does not include `conf.d`, the install fails loudly instead of passing quietly.

**Template unit and installer (`engine/install-engine-service.sh --mode prod`).**
- **Template.** It writes `peertube-engine@.service`, a byte-for-byte copy of today's unit except that `ExecStart` ends in `--host 127.0.0.1 --port %i`. The unit base name stays `peertube-engine`, so `--print-default-service-name` keeps printing it and the instance names are derived as `peertube-engine@<port>`.
- **Port options in prod.** `--port` and `--host` are rejected in prod (fixed pair). `scripts/install-service.sh` stops passing them for the prod contour and refuses `--engine-port` for prod.
- **Install sequence:**
  1. Take the deploy lock (non-blocking; refuse if a deploy is running).
  2. Write the template and listener, and `daemon-reload`.
  3. If the legacy `/etc/systemd/system/peertube-engine.service` exists, stop it, disable it, remove it and `daemon-reload` (migration).
  4. If the snippet is missing, write it naming 7070. If it exists and is valid, keep its port. If it is invalid, fail without touching anything.
  5. Bring up the snippet's instance: start it if not running, restart it only under `--force`, and leave a healthy running one alone without `--force`. Enable it and disable the other instance.
  6. Run `nginx -t`, reload, and check health on 7079.
- **Re-runs.** Never flip the port. A re-run without `--force` on a healthy host only rewrites identical files.
- **`--dry-run`** prints the template, snippet and listener previews and the detected migration and port plan, and writes nothing.

**Client installer.** The prod default `--engine-url` becomes `http://127.0.0.1:7079`, and the central installer's prod `engine_ingest_base` follows it. Dev keeps 7171. The central installer already runs the Engine installer first, so the listener exists before the Client is pointed at it.

**Uninstaller (`engine/uninstall-engine-service.sh --mode prod`).**
- It stops and disables `peertube-engine@7070` and `@7071`, and removes the template and any legacy single unit, so an un-migrated host also uninstalls cleanly.
- It removes the listener and snippet, runs `daemon-reload`, and if nginx is present runs `nginx -t` and reloads. Removing the two files removes the only references to the upstream, so the public site config still validates.
- `--dry-run` lists every action. Dev is untouched.

**Deploy script (`scripts/deploy-bluegreen.sh`).**
- **Repo root.** Found the same way `run-services.sh` and `install-service.sh` find it: `SCRIPT_DIR`, or its parent when `engine/` sits one level up.
- **Options:** `--blue-green` (required), `--timeout <s>` (readiness, default 300, same name as `run-services.sh`), `--warmup <s>` (default 0), `--drain <s>` (default 30), `--dry-run`, `-h|--help`.
- **Drain default of 30 s.** It is the Client's longest Engine request timeout (20 s) plus margin. nginx's graceful reload lets old workers finish their in-flight requests to the old Engine. After 30 s, every request the Client sent before the switch has either finished or been abandoned by the Client itself.
- **Without `--blue-green`:** print usage and exit 2 with no side effects.
- **Root check.** Non-root fails fast except in `--dry-run`. The script checks `id -u` rather than `$EUID`, so tests can stub `id` through PATH and production keeps no bypass flag.
- **Snippet path.** Defaults to `/etc/nginx/peertube-engine-upstream.conf` and can be overridden by one environment variable for tests.
- **Lock file.** `<repo>/engine/server/db/engine-deploy.lock`.
- **Deploy id.** UTC `YYYYmmddTHHMMSSZ-<pid>`. Every line is `deploy_id=… event=… key=value`, printed to stdout and sent through `logger -t peertube-engine-deploy`.
- **Flow (requirements steps 1–11):**
  1. `flock -n` on fd 9 of the lock file.
  2. Refuse if `systemctl is-active peertube-updater.service` reports `active`, `activating`, `deactivating` or `reloading`.
  3. Parse the snippet strictly: exactly one `server 127.0.0.1:(7070|7071);` line.
  4. Stop a leftover target instance if it is not inactive.
  5. `systemctl start peertube-engine@<target>`.
  6. Poll `curl --max-time` on `/api/health` every 2 s. Each round also checks `systemctl is-active` and fails at once on `failed`/`inactive`. 2 s is about 30 requests a minute against the Engine's 60/60 s per-key limit on the fresh instance's own limiter, and a 429 just counts as not ready. Then the optional warm-up sleep and one more health check.
  7. Copy the snippet to a backup beside it, write the new snippet to a temp file in the same directory and `mv` it into place, run `nginx -t`, then `systemctl reload nginx` and log the switch time.
  8. Check `127.0.0.1:7079/api/health` for HTTP 200 whose `X-Engine-Upstream` names the target. Retry about 1 s apart for up to about 10 s, because the reload is asynchronous.
  9. Record the old instance's `MainPID` (`systemctl show -p MainPID --value`). Sleep the drain, stop the old instance, enable the new one, disable the old one.
  10. Remove `engine/server/db/random-cache.tmp.<pid>.db` and its `-journal` sidecar, the same pair `remove_random_cache_temp` deletes.
  11. Exit 0.
- **Phases and rollback.** A phase variable (`pre-switch`, `switching`, `switched`) drives one rollback function. It is called on any failure and from the `INT`/`TERM` traps.
  - `pre-switch`: stop the new instance.
  - `switching`: restore the backup snippet, run `nginx -t`, reload, stop the new instance.
  - `switched`: no rollback; log and mark the exit non-zero.
  - A failure inside rollback logs `ROLLBACK FAILED` with the snippet contents and both instances' states, and exits non-zero.
- **Lock release.** The lock is tied to the open fd, so it is released on every exit, including `SIGKILL`.
- **Client preflight.** Before touching anything, the script refuses if `/etc/systemd/system/peertube-client.service` exists and does not contain `--engine-url http://127.0.0.1:7079`. A flip would otherwise cut off a Client that still points straight at 7070. This guard is my addition: it touches nothing and is listed under Tradeoffs.
- **`--dry-run`** prints the deploy id, active and target ports, updater state, Client preflight result and the ordered action list. It takes no lock and writes, starts, stops and reloads nothing.

**Updater (`updater-worker.py`).**
- **New argument.** It gains `--engine-upstream-snippet <path>`; the prod updater installer writes it into the prod unit. With it set:
  - The worker takes `fcntl.flock` on the deploy lock (`--deploy-lock-file`, defaulting to the same repo-relative path), polling non-blocking up to a bounded wait of 30 minutes. If the wait runs out it fails before stopping anything.
  - Once it holds the lock, it parses the snippet with the same strict rule as the deploy script, resolves `peertube-engine@<port>` once into a local variable, stops that unit, and in the existing `finally` starts the same unit. It releases the lock after the start.
- **Without the argument** the behaviour is byte-for-byte today's, so dev is unchanged.
- **Overlap in both directions.** The deploy refuses while the updater unit is running, and the updater cannot stop or start while a deploy holds the lock.
- **Sudoers.** In prod the updater installer writes exactly four `NOPASSWD` entries: `<systemctl> stop|start peertube-engine@7070|7071`. Sudoers matches arguments literally, so the worker must call the unit without the `.service` suffix, exactly as written there. Dev keeps its single-name rule.

**Docs.** `DEPLOYMENT.md` gets every section the requirements list:
- the units table (template instances replace `peertube-engine.service` in prod);
- "Day to day": the deploy command, and how to find the active instance (`cat` the snippet);
- §6: the 7079 listener and the snippet; 7079 stays loopback-only; Firewall says never open 7070, 7071, 7072 or 7079;
- the updater section: it stops and starts the active instance;
- Triage rows for: lock held, readiness timeout, nginx validation failure and rollback, finding the active port;
- the Client `--engine-url` in prod;
- §7: `seed=` goes to the active port.

`README.md`, `engine/server/README.md` and `UPDATER_WORKER.md` are brought in line wherever the impact inventory finds the prod unit name or 7070 named as the only prod port.

**How each requirement is met.**
- **No outage window:** the Client talks to a fixed 7079 and nginx flips the upstream only after the new instance is healthy.
- **One command and automatic rollback:** the phase machine above.
- **Snippet as single source of truth:** the deploy, installer and updater all read only the snippet.
- **One instance enabled:** the installer and deploy step 9 keep enablement equal to the snippet.
- **Updater compatibility:** the snippet argument, the shared lock and the four-entry sudoers rule.
- **Logging:** one tag, `deploy_id` on every line, and the required fields as `key=value` pairs.
- **Dev contour:** untouched, because every new behaviour is gated on `--mode prod` or on the updater's new argument.

**Validation.**
- **New `tests/active/test_deploy_bluegreen.py`** copies the script into a temp tree (`scripts/` and `engine/server/db/`) and runs it with a stub `bin/` on PATH:
  - `systemctl` logs calls and answers `is-active` and `MainPID` from scripted state files;
  - `nginx -t` passes or fails on a toggle;
  - `curl` returns scripted statuses and the `X-Engine-Upstream` header per URL;
  - `logger` records lines;
  - `id` prints 0.
  - It covers every case in the requirements list. Lock contention is tested by holding `fcntl.flock` on the lock path from the test process.
- **`test_updater_worker.py` additions:** snippet parsing (valid, missing, foreign port), unit resolution, and that stop and start use the same resolved name. The existing AST test (`systemctl_cmd(action="start")` inside a `finally`) must still pass, so the structure is kept.
- **Installer test:** a pytest runs the Engine and updater installers with `--dry-run` against a fake project tree (stub `venv/bin/python3` and `server.py`) and asserts the template's `--port %i`, the four exact sudoers entries, and the 7079 default in the Client installer.

### Alternatives considered

- **Keep the Client pointed at a port and restart the Client on each flip.** Rejected by the operator topology, and a Client restart is itself a gap.
- **Swap the port in place with `SO_REUSEPORT` or socket activation.** This needs Engine changes and gives no clean drain or rollback point. nginx is already on the host.
- **State file or `systemctl` query as the source of the active port.** The requirements forbid it, and two sources can disagree. The snippet is what nginx actually uses, so it cannot drift from traffic.
- **Upstream with both servers and `down`/`backup` markers.** It saves nothing over rewriting one line, and it breaks "the upstream names exactly one server at every moment".
- **`nginx -s reload` vs `systemctl reload nginx`.** Both are asynchronous. The systemd form matches how the host runs nginx and is just as easy to stub.
- **Post-switch check on a plain 200.** Rejected: right after an async reload, a 200 can come from an old worker still proxying to the old Engine, which is alive, so a broken switch would pass. Identifying the upstream through `X-Engine-Upstream` closes that hole without adding an instance field to the Engine.
- **Lock file in `/run/lock`.** Rejected. With `fs.protected_regular` on (the default on current distros), root opening with `O_CREAT` a lock file the service user created in that sticky, world-writable directory is refused, which would make deploy and updater block each other. The repo's `engine/server/db/` is owned by the service user and not sticky. Both sides can create or open the file there, and both derive the path from the repo root with no configuration.
- **Updater fails at once if a deploy holds the lock.** Rejected in favour of a bounded wait: the crawl before that point takes hours, and a deploy takes minutes.
- **Updater finds the active instance through the deploy script (`--print-active-port`).** Rejected. It would couple a Python job to a root-oriented shell script. The snippet format is one line, so two small parsers with one shared test fixture is the cheaper simplification. Ceiling: a format change must touch both. Upgrade path: move the parser into one helper both call.
- **Deploy pulls code or restarts the Client.** Out of scope by requirement.

### Gotchas and risks

- **Oneshot updater state.** `peertube-updater.service` is `Type=oneshot`, so while it runs `is-active` prints `activating`, not `active`. Checking only for `active` would let a deploy start mid-run.
- **Async reload.** Covered by the `X-Engine-Upstream` check with a short retry window. The retry has to be bounded, and failing it takes the full rollback path.
- **`Restart=on-failure` during readiness.** A crashing new instance cycles through `activating (auto-restart)`. Readiness treats only `failed`/`inactive` as an immediate failure. A crash loop runs until the readiness timeout, then rolls back.
- **Behaviour change while the Engine is down.** During the updater's stop/merge window the Client now gets an nginx 502 instead of a refused connection. The Client's Engine-down handling and `/api/health` reporting must treat both the same. The impact step should confirm this in `client/backend/server.py` around its `URLError`/`RemoteDisconnected` handling.
- **nginx becomes a hard dependency of the prod Engine install.** The install fails cleanly without it. If `nginx.conf` lacks the `conf.d` include, the post-install check on 7079 reports it.
- **One-time migration outage.** Moving from `peertube-engine.service` to `@7070` means stopping the old unit before the instance can bind 7070. Pointing the Client at 7079 means restarting the Client once. Both are inherent to the migration, not to deploys.
- **Reboot inside the drain window.** If the host reboots during the drain, the old instance is still the enabled one while the snippet names the new. That follows from the specified step-9 order: about 30 s of exposure per deploy, and the next deploy or an installer run converges it. Upgrade path: enable the new instance right after step 8.
- **The central installer passes `--force` for prod by default.** Re-running it restarts the active instance in place, which is today's behaviour. Restarting without downtime is what the deploy command is for, and the docs say so.
- **The smoke script is broken before this build.** `tests/run-installers-smoke.sh` points at `${ROOT_DIR}/install-service.sh` and the root-level `install-service-prod.sh`/`-dev.sh` wrappers, which no longer exist (the scripts live in `scripts/`). It therefore exits before its checks even in `--dry-run-only`, and it is not in the gating suite. The new contract checks go in pytest so they actually run. Fixing the smoke paths, plus its prod `engine_ingest_base`, engine unit name and port expectations, is a small adjacent fix to schedule separately, not to fold in silently.
- **Lock fd inheritance.** The script launches nothing long-lived, and systemd spawns the Engines, so no child keeps fd 9 open past the script's exit.

### Tradeoffs the operator accepts

- An extra loopback nginx hop on every Client→Engine request, which also adds nginx to the Engine path's failure surface.
- A 30 s default drain and 2 s readiness poll, which make every deploy take at least `startup + 30 s`.
- The updater can wait up to 30 minutes for a running deploy before it fails without touching anything.
- Two copies of the snippet parser, one bash and one Python (named simplification above).
- Two small additions beyond the letter of the requirements, both refusals or tighter checks that never change state:
  - the Client-URL preflight refusal;
  - the stricter post-switch check (200 and the target named in `X-Engine-Upstream`).
- A response header (`X-Engine-Upstream`) on the internal listener only. The Client never forwards it.

Recorded ungated, at the operator direction.

### impacts

<impacts>
<impact path="scripts/deploy-bluegreen.sh" element="new script (the whole file)">
**What changes.** A new root-run bash script. It finds the repo root with the same `SCRIPT_DIR`/parent rule as `scripts/run-services.sh:24-29` and `scripts/install-service.sh:4-9`. It takes `--blue-green`, `--timeout`, `--warmup`, `--drain`, `--dry-run` and `-h`. The lock is `flock -n` on fd 9 of `<repo>/engine/server/db/engine-deploy.lock`. The phase machine is `pre-switch`, `switching`, `switched` with one rollback function and `INT`/`TERM` traps. Log lines go to stdout and through `logger -t peertube-engine-deploy`. It reads and writes the snippet `/etc/nginx/peertube-engine-upstream.conf`, overridable by one env var.

**What it depends on.**
- The snippet and listener the Engine installer writes.
- The `peertube-engine@.service` template, whose instance name is the port.
- The Engine's `/api/health`: it is in `_dispatch_get`, `engine/server/api/handlers/similar.py:469-479`, and it is rate-limited per `ip:path` key at 60 per 60 s (`server_config.py:482-483`).
- `curl` sends no `X-Client-IP`, so readiness polls, the warm-up re-check and the post-switch retries all land in the new instance's `127.0.0.1:/api/health` bucket. That is about 30 + 1 + up to 10 requests in a 60 s window: inside 60, but with little margin. A tighter retry loop or a shorter poll interval would turn a healthy instance into 429 "not ready".
- The temp file name contract of `random_cache_temp_path` (`engine/server/data/random_cache.py:197-205`): `random-cache.tmp.<pid>.db` plus `-journal`. Bash re-implements it.
- The updater unit name `peertube-updater.service`. While it runs, `is-active` reports `activating`, because the unit is `Type=oneshot` (`engine/install-updater-service.sh:333`).
- The Client unit file `/etc/systemd/system/peertube-client.service`, for the preflight. `client/install-client-service.sh:197` writes `--engine-url ${ENGINE_URL}` verbatim. The exact-string preflight therefore refuses an equivalent URL such as `http://localhost:7079` or one with a trailing `/`, and it never checks a Client installed under a custom `--service-name`.

**Risk of regression.**
- **Rollback correctness.** A wrong phase at the moment of failure either stops the only serving instance or leaves a snippet nginx has not loaded.
- **A foreign listener fools readiness.** If something other than the systemd instance holds the target port, for example a manual `scripts/run-services.sh --engine-port 7071` run or a stray test Engine, `curl` gets a 200 while the unit sits in `activating (auto-restart)` after a bind failure. Readiness then passes on the wrong process. Only `failed`/`inactive` trip the immediate failure.
- **Lock held after SIGKILL.** fd 9 is inherited by short-lived children (`sleep` during the drain, `curl`, `logger`). A SIGKILL during the drain keeps the lock held until that `sleep` exits. That is bounded, but it contradicts "released on every exit" in the strict sense.
- **Lock file ownership.** If root creates the lock file first, it is root-owned `0644` in the service user's directory. Any updater open that needs write access then fails (see the updater entry).
- **No production precedent.** The script is new, so nothing existing regresses. The cost of a bug falls on live traffic at the next deploy.
</impact>
<impact path="engine/install-engine-service.sh" element="install_engine_service(): prod branch (template unit, migration, instance bring-up, health check)">

The rest of the unit content stays byte-identical. Dev keeps today's lines 170-244 unchanged.

New in prod:
- the deploy-lock acquisition;
- the legacy-unit migration (stop, disable, `rm`, `daemon-reload` of `peertube-engine.service`);
- the snippet read/create/validate step;
- the instance bring-up: start if not running, restart only under `--force`, enable it and disable the other instance;
- `nginx -t`, reload, and a 7079 health check.

**Existing code that must change.**
- The `--force` block (lines 205-214) stops, disables and `rm`s `${ENGINE_SERVICE_NAME}.service`. In prod it must target the instance and the template instead.
- The enable/restart and verification lines (222-244) use `${ENGINE_SERVICE_NAME}.service` for `is-enabled`, `is-active`, `journalctl -u` and the printed Status/Logs hints. They must use `peertube-engine@<port>`.
- The non-dry-run requirements (lines 163-167) gain `nginx`, `flock` and `curl` in prod.

**Risk of regression.**
- **One-time migration outage.** The migration stops the live prod Engine.
- **`--force` restarts the active instance.** The central installer passes `--force` for prod by default (`scripts/install-service.sh:270-273`), so every central re-run restarts the active instance in place, which is today's behaviour.

- **Lock path from `PROJECT_DIR`.** The lock path is derived from `PROJECT_DIR` (after `realpath`, line 308). The deploy script derives it from its own `SCRIPT_DIR`. A `--project-dir` that differs from the checkout the deploy runs from gives two different locks.
</impact>
<impact path="engine/install-engine-service.sh" element="argument parsing (--host/--port), print_usage, resolve_default_engine_port">
**What changes.**
- `--host` and `--port` (lines 265-272) are rejected when `--mode prod`.
- `DEFAULT_PROD_ENGINE_PORT=7070` (line 23) and `resolve_default_engine_port` (lines 111-118) no longer drive the prod unit: the port comes from the snippet, or 7070 on first install.
- The usage text (lines 35-36 and 44) says `prod: service=peertube-engine host=127.0.0.1 port=7070` and `--port ... (default: 7070 prod...)`. It must describe the template, the 7070/7071 pair and the nginx files.

**What depends on it.**
- `scripts/install-service.sh` passes `--host` and `--port` unconditionally (lines 315-316), so the central installer must stop passing them for prod in the same change.
- `tests/run-installers-smoke.sh` (`help_install_engine`) relies on `--help`.

**Risk of regression.** If the central installer and the Engine installer are changed in different phases, `install-service.sh --mode prod` breaks: the new rejection fails it. Dev must keep accepting both options, because the smoke script's dev path and DEPLOYMENT.md examples pass `--port 7171`.
</impact>
<impact path="engine/install-engine-service.sh" element="generated nginx files: /etc/nginx/peertube-engine-upstream.conf and /etc/nginx/conf.d/peertube-engine-internal.conf">
**What changes.** New content written by the prod installer.

The snippet holds one line, `upstream peertube_engine { server 127.0.0.1:<port>; }`.

The listener:
- has `listen 127.0.0.1:7079` and includes the snippet by absolute path;
- does `location / { proxy_pass http://peertube_engine; }`;
- sets `proxy_set_header Host $http_host` and `client_max_body_size` ≥ 1 000 000;
- adds `add_header X-Engine-Upstream $upstream_addr`;
- has no upstream keepalive.

**What depends on it.**
- The deploy script: it parses the snippet and checks the `X-Engine-Upstream` value.
- The updater: it parses the snippet.
- The Client, through `--engine-url http://127.0.0.1:7079`.

**Verified facts the design relies on.**
- None of the forwarded custom headers contain underscores, so nginx's default `underscores_in_headers off` does not drop them. The headers are `x-client-ip` (`client/backend/server.py:599`), `X-Bridge-Token` (`client/backend/lib/engine_api_client.py:10`) and the future `X-Request-ID`.
- The Client's largest request body is bounded at 1 000 000 bytes (`client/backend/server.py:80`). The internal bodies are far smaller: at most 1 000 dislikes and 50 client likes.
- With a single server in an upstream, nginx ignores `max_fails` and `fail_timeout`. One Engine error therefore never makes the upstream "unavailable" for 10 s.

**Risk of regression.**
- **`add_header` and 5xx responses.** `add_header` without `always` is not emitted on nginx-generated 5xx responses. The post-switch check only looks for it on 200, so this is fine, but an implementer adding `always` changes nothing harmful.
- **Shared access log.** The listener's access lines go to the default `access.log`, which the public `:80` site also uses. Without a separate `access_log` for 7079, the operator validation "no 5xx spikes in the public site's access log" mixes in internal hops. A 502 during the updater's stop window on 7079 would read as a public spike.
- **A non-loopback `listen` would expose the Engine.** The Engine has no authentication and `/internal/*` accepts writes.
</impact>
<impact path="engine/uninstall-engine-service.sh" element="whole script (prod branch)">
**What changes.**
- Prod stops and disables `peertube-engine@7070` and `@7071`.
- It removes `peertube-engine@.service`, any legacy `peertube-engine.service`, the listener and the snippet.
- It runs `daemon-reload` and `reset-failed`, then `nginx -t` and a reload if nginx exists.
- Today (lines 105-141) it stops, disables and removes one `${ENGINE_SERVICE_NAME}.service`. Dev keeps that.
- `MODE` defaults to `prod` here (line 7), unlike the installers.

**Existing quirk.** Lines 130 and 132 send `run_cmd ... >/dev/null 2>&1`. In `--dry-run` this swallows the `[dry-run]` echo of the stop/disable lines, so today's dry-run lists only the `rm`. The requirement that `--dry-run` list every action means the new lines must not copy that redirect.

**What depends on it.**
- `scripts/uninstall-service.sh:243-257`. It always passes `--service-name peertube-engine` for prod and runs the Client uninstaller first, so the Client is down before the listener goes.
- The smoke matrix (`dry_uninstall_engine_prod` greps for `peertube-engine`).

**Risk of regression.**
- An un-migrated host must still uninstall cleanly.
- Removing the snippet before the listener, with nginx then reloaded in between, would fail `nginx -t`, because the listener includes a missing file. The order must be listener first, or both removed before any test or reload.
- With nginx absent the uninstall must not fail.
</impact>
<impact path="engine/install-updater-service.sh" element="updater_exec, sudoers rule (dry-run preview line 364 and written rule line 376), print_usage">
**What changes.**
- In prod, `updater_exec` (line 324) gains `--engine-upstream-snippet /etc/nginx/peertube-engine-upstream.conf`, and optionally `--deploy-lock-file`.
- The sudoers line is today `${SERVICE_USER} ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: ${systemctl_bin} stop ${ENGINE_SERVICE_NAME}, ${systemctl_bin} start ${ENGINE_SERVICE_NAME}`. It appears twice, identically: the dry-run preview at line 364 and the file at line 376. In prod it becomes exactly four entries, `stop|start peertube-engine@7070|7071`. Both copies must change together.
- Dev keeps its single-name rule.
- The usage text (line 40, `prod: engine=peertube-engine`) gets updated.

**What depends on it.**
- `scripts/install-service.sh:install_updater_for_contour`.
- `engine/install-engine-service.sh:install_updater_with_timer`.
- `visudo -cf` validation (line 377).
- `scripts/uninstall-service.sh:181`, which removes `/etc/sudoers.d/${updater_service_name}-systemctl`. That file name is unchanged.

**Risk of regression.**
- **Literal sudoers match.** Sudoers matches arguments literally. If the worker ever passes `peertube-engine@7070.service`, or the rule names a `.service` suffix the worker omits, `sudo -n` fails mid-pipeline after the merge has started. The start in the `finally` would fail too, leaving prod down.
- **Literal name or derived name.** If the four entries are derived from `${ENGINE_SERVICE_NAME}@<port>`, an `--engine-service-name` override in prod changes them. If they are written literally, the override is silently ignored. Either way, decide it explicitly.
- **Dry-run needs `systemctl`.** Even in `--dry-run`, lines 275-278 require `systemctl` on PATH, a real `${PROJECT_DIR}/engine/server/db/jobs/updater-worker.py` and an executable `venv/bin/python3`. Line 239 requires an existing `--service-user`. The planned dry-run pytest needs a stub `systemctl` on PATH and an existing user, for example the current user.
</impact>
<impact path="scripts/install-service.sh" element="install_contour() prod branch, --engine-port/--engine-host handling, DEFAULT_PROD_ENGINE_PORT, print_usage">
**What changes.**
- For `contour=prod`, `engine_cmd` (lines 308-317) stops passing `--host` and `--port`.
- `engine_ingest_base` (lines 298-302) becomes `http://127.0.0.1:7079` instead of `http://${engine_host}:${engine_port}`.

- `DEFAULT_PROD_ENGINE_PORT=7070` (line 45) loses meaning for prod.
- The check that the Engine and Client ports differ (lines 294-296) and the echo lines (305-306) need to make sense without a prod engine port.
- In `--mode all`, `ensure_single_contour_overrides_only` already forbids overrides, so prod in `all` is fine.

**What depends on it.** Operators, DEPLOYMENT.md and README.md (`sudo bash install-service.sh --mode prod`), and the smoke script (`dry_install_prod_engine_port` expects `127.0.0.1:7070`; that script is already broken).

**Risk of regression.**

<impact path="scripts/uninstall-service.sh" element="uninstall_contour() / engine_cmd">
**What changes.** Possibly nothing in code. It keeps passing `--service-name peertube-engine` (lines 243-249), and the Engine uninstaller derives the instances and nginx files in prod. The `print_usage` text could mention that prod now also removes the nginx listener and snippet.

**What depends on it.** Operators; `tests/run-installers-smoke.sh` (broken paths).

</impact>
<impact path="client/install-client-service.sh" element="DEFAULT_PROD_ENGINE_PORT and ENGINE_URL default; print_usage example">
**What changes.**
- The prod default `ENGINE_URL` (lines 162-168) becomes `http://127.0.0.1:7079`. Today `DEFAULT_PROD_ENGINE_PORT=7070` at line 20 feeds it. Dev stays at `7171`.
- The usage example on line 46 (`--mode prod --engine-url http://127.0.0.1:7070`) becomes 7079.

**What depends on it.**

- `scripts/install-service.sh` always passes `--engine-url` explicitly, so the central path depends on the change there, not here.
- `tests/run-installers-smoke.sh:827` checks that `--engine-url` appears in `--help`.

</impact>
<impact path="client/backend/server.py" element="_proxy_engine_request() HTTPError vs URLError branches (lines 576-754); DEFAULT_ENGINE_INGEST_BASE (line 46)">
**What changes.** No code change is planned. This entry is the behaviour check the plan asked for.

**What happens today.** When the Engine is down, the Client gets a refused connection. `urlopen` raises `URLError`, which goes to lines 703-708: one retry after 0.25 s (`ENGINE_PROXY_RETRY_COUNT=1`, line 81). After that, a JSON 502 `{"error":"Engine read proxy failed","code":"ENGINE_PROXY_UNAVAILABLE"}`.

**What happens behind nginx.** When the Engine is down (the updater's stop window, or a crash), nginx answers its own 502 with an HTML body. `urlopen` raises `HTTPError`, which goes to lines 655-686. The payload is non-empty, so the Client passes status 502 and nginx's `content-type: text/html` body straight to the browser. It makes no retry and gives no `ENGINE_PROXY_UNAVAILABLE` code. The log records `"proxy request completed"` with `status=502` at INFO, not `"proxy request unavailable"` at WARNING.

An Engine that drops a connection, for example the migrate-whitelist Triage case, likewise becomes an nginx 502 HTML page instead of the `except Exception` branch's JSON `ENGINE_PROXY_FAILURE`.

**What depends on it.** The frontend. `client/frontend/src/data/videos.ts:152-160` checks `!response.ok` first and wraps `response.json()` in try/catch, so an HTML 502 degrades to the default message. The other data modules (`search.ts`, `blocks.ts`, `profile.ts` and others) were not read line by line. Uncertain: a module that calls `.json()` before checking `ok` would throw a parse error instead of showing the message.

**Risk of regression.**
- **Outward behaviour.** Medium. The status stays 502, but the body, the log level and the retry change. Alerting or log filters keyed on `ENGINE_PROXY_UNAVAILABLE` or the WARNING line go quiet during Engine outages.
- **Possible follow-up.** A small Client change would restore today's handling: treat an `HTTPError` 502/503/504 whose content-type is not JSON as a transport error. It is outside the plan's "nothing in Python server changes", so it needs an explicit decision.
- **`/api/health`.** The Client's `/api/health` (lines 289-299) never probes the Engine and only echoes `engine_ingest_base`. Its reporting is unaffected, except that it will show `http://127.0.0.1:7079`.
- **`DEFAULT_ENGINE_INGEST_BASE`.** Stays at 7070, for manual and dev runs and `scripts/run-services.sh`. Correct per scope.
</impact>
<impact path="client/backend/lib/engine_api_client.py" element="_post_json() HTTPError handling; bridge_headers()">
**What changes.** No code change. Behind nginx, an Engine-down call to `/internal/videos/resolve`, `/internal/videos/metadata` or `/internal/dislikes/centroids` arrives as `HTTPError` 502 with an HTML body instead of `URLError`.
- `_post_json` (lines 49-59) swallows the `JSONDecodeError` and returns `(502, {})`.
- The callers raise `EngineApiError("... (HTTP 502): unknown error")` instead of the transport message.
- `_publish_to_engine_bridge` (`client/backend/server.py:1073-1076`) logs `engine bridge HTTP 502` instead of `engine bridge unavailable`.

**What depends on it.** `_respond_engine_failure` and the like/profile routes. The outward status is still a fixed-text 502.

**Risk of regression.** Low. Only the log text differs. `X-Bridge-Token` passes through nginx unchanged: it has a hyphen, no underscore.
</impact>
<impact path="engine/server/db/jobs/updater-worker.py" element="parse_args(): new --engine-upstream-snippet and --deploy-lock-file">
**What changes.** Two new options. `--deploy-lock-file` defaults to `repo_root / "engine/server/db/engine-deploy.lock"`, where `repo_root = script_dir.parents[3]` as on line 84. `--service-name` and `resolve_default_engine_service_name` (lines 38-79, 291-292) stay for dev and the no-snippet path.

**What depends on it.** The prod unit's `ExecStart` written by `engine/install-updater-service.sh:324`. `engine/server/db/jobs/tests/test-orchestrator-smoke.py:422-467` builds an updater command without the new argument, so it keeps today's behaviour.

**Risk of regression.** Low, provided the option is absent by default so behaviour without it is byte-for-byte today's. A name clash with the existing `--lock-file` (line 169, the updater's own single-run lock in `/tmp`) is the obvious confusion. Keep both names distinct and documented.
</impact>
<impact path="engine/server/db/jobs/updater-worker.py" element="main(): service stop/start try/finally (lines 1261-1345), plus new snippet-parse and deploy-lock helpers">
**What changes.** With the snippet argument set:
- take `fcntl.flock` non-blocking on the deploy lock, polling for up to 30 minutes, and fail before the stop if the wait runs out;
- parse the snippet strictly, accepting only `server 127.0.0.1:7070;` or `7071;`;
- resolve `peertube-engine@<port>` once into a local;
- stop it, and in the existing `finally` start the same local;
- release the lock after the start.

**What depends on it.**
- `systemctl_cmd` (lines 409-420) builds `[systemctl, action, name]` with no `.service` suffix, which the four literal sudoers entries require.
- `tests/active/test_updater_worker.py::test_main_runs_similarity_stage_after_service_start` (lines 307-326) needs exactly one `ast.Try` in `main` whose `finalbody` contains `systemctl_cmd(action="start")`. `run_similarity_stage` must be called once, after that try's `end_lineno`. That try must contain the `build-ann-index.py` constant and a `run_with_cpu_fallback` call, and no `similarity_precompute_cmd`/`run_similarity_stage`. Any refactor that wraps the start in a helper, splits the try, or puts the lock-release `finally` around the similarity stage breaks this test.
- `test_updater_main_uses_builder` (lines 78-89) scans module constants. It is unaffected.

**Risk of regression: high.**
- **Lock file permissions.** The deploy and the installer run as root and may create `engine-deploy.lock` first, as root-owned `0644`. The updater runs as the service user (`User=${SERVICE_USER}`, `install-updater-service.sh:334`). Opening the lock with any write mode (`open(path, "a")`, `O_RDWR`, `O_WRONLY`) raises `PermissionError`, and the prod pipeline dies after hours of crawling. It must open `O_RDONLY | O_CREAT`; `flock` works on a read-only fd.
- **Where the stop sits.** If the lock is taken or the snippet parsed inside the try after `service_stopped=True`, a failure there must not start the wrong unit. Resolve the name before the stop.
- **Lock held through the merge.** The lock is held through merge, popularity and the ANN rebuild, which can take tens of minutes. A deploy started then fails at `flock -n`, which is intended.
- **Failed start in the `finally`.** If the start fails, the lock must still be released, or the next deploy is blocked until the updater process exits. The process exits soon after, so the risk is bounded.
- **Leftover random-cache temp file.** The updater's stop of the active instance can now leave `random-cache.tmp.<pid>.db` behind, as before. Nothing new.
</impact>
<impact path="engine/server/api/handlers/similar.py" element="_get_client_ip(), _rate_limit_check(), /api/health in _dispatch_get (lines 315-330, 465-479, 604-611)">
**What changes.** No code change.

**What depends on it.**
- The Client's `X-Client-IP` passes through nginx unchanged, so the per-visitor buckets keep working.
- Requests without `X-Client-IP` now see the peer as nginx's `127.0.0.1` instead of the Client's `127.0.0.1`. That is the same key, so there is no change.
- The deploy's `curl` probes, direct on `<target>` and via 7079, all key on `127.0.0.1:/api/health`, at 60 per 60 s.
- `_get_full_url` logs `Host`. With `proxy_set_header Host $http_host`, the Engine's access-log URLs will show `127.0.0.1:7079`.

**Risk of regression.** Low. This is where the deploy's poll and retry budget must fit (see the deploy entry). The docstring (lines 318-321) rests trust on "the Engine binds loopback and the gateway is its only reachable peer". nginx on 7079 is now a second loopback path that forwards the header verbatim. That is an equivalent trust boundary, since both are loopback-only, but ADR-0002 should note it.
</impact>
<impact path="engine/server/api/server.py" element="main(): argparse --host/--port, SIGTERM handling, random-cache worker start (lines 169-179, 296-311, 493-542)">
**What changes.** No code change. Two instances of the same checkout run at once during a deploy.

Verified:
- There is no single-instance lock or PID file keyed on the port.
- The FAISS index is opened with `IO_FLAG_MMAP | IO_FLAG_READ_ONLY` (line 350), so the page cache is shared.
- SIGTERM becomes a graceful `KeyboardInterrupt` (lines 298-311) and closes the server.
- The random-cache worker is a daemon thread, so a stop mid-build leaves `random-cache.tmp.<pid>.db` behind. That is why deploy step 10 exists.

**What depends on it.** The template's `--port %i`; readiness on `/api/health`.

**Risk of regression.**
- **Memory.** Each instance loads its own Python process and the CPU `SentenceTransformer` query encoder (`data/query_encoder.py:36-90`). Peak RSS during the overlap is roughly double for those parts. That is not mentioned in the accepted tradeoffs; it is an operator-host sizing risk.
- **Two startup cache builds.** Both instances' startup random-cache builds scan `whitelist.db` concurrently. This is accepted by the requirements.
- **Ingest overlap.** During the drain, bridge ingests can reach both instances. SQLite handles it with locks. Each instance's first ingest after start runs a raw-event prune, as on any restart today.
</impact>
<impact path="engine/server/data/random_cache.py" element="random_cache_temp_path() / remove_random_cache_temp() (lines 197-205)">
**What changes.** No code change. The deploy script re-implements the name `<stem>.tmp.<pid><suffix>` → `engine/server/db/random-cache.tmp.<MainPID>.db` and the `-journal` sidecar in bash.

**What depends on it.** Deploy step 10 and the tests asserting its removal.

**Risk of regression.** Low. Any future rename of the temp pattern here silently stops the deploy's cleanup. No test ties the two together unless the new deploy test derives the name from this function. It does not, since it copies the script into a temp tree.
</impact>
<impact path="engine/server/api/server_config.py" element="DEFAULT_SERVER_PORT (line 412), DEFAULT_RATE_LIMIT_MAX_REQUESTS/WINDOW (lines 482-483), DEFAULT_RANDOM_CACHE_DB_PATH (line 418)">
**What changes.** Nothing. `DEFAULT_SERVER_PORT=7070` stays: it is used by manual runs and `run-services.sh`, and the template always passes `--port`. The 60/60 s limit is what the deploy's 2 s poll is sized against.

<impact path="engine/watch-engine-logs.sh" element="-prod flag → UNIT=peertube-engine.service (lines 12, 72, 151-155)">

After migration `peertube-engine.service` no longer exists, so `journalctl -u peertube-engine.service -f` shows nothing for prod: it fails silently, with no error. It should follow the instances, for example `journalctl -u 'peertube-engine@*'` (journalctl accepts globs for `-u`) or both instance units. The help text on line 12 changes accordingly.

<impact path="scripts/run-services.sh" element="ENGINE_PORT=7070 default (line 38)">

<impact path="tests/active/test_deploy_bluegreen.py" element="new test module">
**What changes.** New pytest. <impact path="tests/active/test_updater_worker.py" element="new snippet-parse / unit-resolution tests; existing AST tests (lines 78-89, 307-326)">

### highest_risk

engine/server/db/jobs/updater-worker.py main() stop/start: it runs unattended in prod after hours of crawling. If it opens the deploy lock in write mode when root already created the file, the run fails with PermissionError. A sudoers mismatch between the four literal entries and the worker's unit name (for example a stray `.service` suffix) makes even the `finally` start fail and leaves prod with no Engine. The single-try/finally shape is also pinned by test_main_runs_similarity_stage_after_service_start.
engine/install-engine-service.sh prod branch: it does a one-time migration that stops the live Engine, makes nginx and a `conf.d` include hard prerequisites, and must never flip or restart a healthy instance except under `--force`. The central installer passes `--force` for prod by default. The installer also has to change in lockstep with scripts/install-service.sh, which today always passes the `--host`/`--port` that prod will now reject.
scripts/deploy-bluegreen.sh: a new root script whose phase/rollback machine edits live nginx config. A wrong phase on failure stops the only serving instance or leaves an unloaded snippet. Its readiness check can be fooled by a foreign process on the target port. Its poll and retry budget shares the new instance's 60-per-minute `127.0.0.1:/api/health` rate-limit bucket.

## 2026-09-30 - Step 4 - Reassess the implementation plan (pass 1)

Pass 1. New impacts: YES.

I checked the inventory against the files it names: both Engine installers and the uninstaller, the central install and uninstall scripts, the Client installer, the Client proxy, `engine_api_client`, the updater's `main()`, `parse_args` and `systemctl_cmd`, the AST test, `random_cache.py`, `watch-engine-logs.sh`, `.gitignore`, DEPLOYMENT §6 and the frontend data modules. Every line reference I opened matched. Two points the inventory left uncertain are now settled. First, every frontend module that reads Client responses checks `response.ok` before calling `.json()`, or wraps `.json()` in try/catch: `blocks`, `cache`, `profile`, `reactions`, `search`, `user-actions`, `user-profile`, `videos` and both page modules. So nginx's HTML 502 page degrades to the default error message everywhere and never throws a parse error. Second, the Engine reads `Host` only for logging, in `_get_full_url` (similar.py:334), so `Host: 127.0.0.1:7079` changes log text and nothing else. I found one new impact: a deploy can leave the snippet unreadable by the updater. One known risk deserves a direct guard: a manual `server.py --dev` binds 7071 by default (`DEV_SERVER_PORT = 7071`, server.py:141), which is exactly the "foreign listener" case the inventory describes. Neither changes the plan's shape.
<question id="1">
    Yes, with two caveats the plan does not yet close. (a) Step 7 writes the new snippet to a temp file and moves it into place. If that temp file comes from `mktemp`, it is root-owned with mode 0600. nginx's master runs as root and loads it fine, so the deploy succeeds. But the updater runs as the service user (`User=${SERVICE_USER}`, install-updater-service.sh:334) and cannot read it. From the first deploy onward, every nightly updater run fails at the snippet parse. It fails before the stop, so nothing breaks visibly, but the data never updates again. (b) Readiness accepts a 200 from any process on the target port and only fails at once on `failed`/`inactive`. A manual `server.py --dev`, which defaults to 7071, or a `run-services.sh --engine-port 7071` run makes the new instance's bind fail and loop in `activating (auto-restart)`. Readiness then passes on the stray process, the `X-Engine-Upstream` check passes too because the address is right, and the deploy stops the real old instance. Production is then served by a hand-started process. The requirements' conflicts note says a `--dev` run makes readiness fail; the tree shows it can pass instead. Everything else holds against the code. The updater's single try/finally (updater-worker.py:1261-1345) can resolve the unit name before the stop without breaking the AST test. `systemctl_cmd` adds no `.service` suffix, which matches the four literal sudoers entries. The Engine's `_get_client_ip` trust and rate-limit keys are unchanged behind nginx. The random-cache temp path is fixed, `engine/server/db/random-cache.db` with no env override, so step 10's bash copy of the name is correct.
</question>
<question id="2">
    nginx becomes a hard dependency of the prod Engine path, and of the prod install. The prod host migrates once: the Engine stops while `@7070` takes over, and the Client restarts once onto 7079. Every Client-to-Engine request gains a loopback hop. While the Engine is down (the updater's merge window, or a crash), the Client relays nginx's HTML 502 instead of its own JSON `ENGINE_PROXY_UNAVAILABLE`. That means no 0.25 s retry, an INFO "proxy request completed" log line instead of a WARNING, and bridge errors logged as `HTTP 502` instead of `unavailable`. The browser behaviour is verified harmless. A deploy holds two Engine processes for at least `startup + 30 s`, so query-encoder and Python memory roughly double for that window. Deploys are refused while the updater unit is running, which includes the hours-long crawl. The updater can wait up to 30 minutes for a deploy. If the 7079 listener gets no `access_log` of its own, its lines land in the public site's access log.
</question>
<question id="3">
    Everything the inventory lists, plus the following:
- The engine and central installers change in one phase. The central installer passes `--host`/`--port` unconditionally (install-service.sh:315-316), and the Engine installer will now reject them.
- Both sudoers copies change together: the dry-run preview (install-updater-service.sh:364) and the written rule (line 376).
- The updater opens the deploy lock `O_RDONLY|O_CREAT`.
- The updater resolves the instance before `service_stopped = True`.
- The uninstaller's new lines drop the `>/dev/null 2>&1` redirect (uninstall-engine-service.sh:130/132) that hides dry-run output.
- `watch-engine-logs.sh -prod` follows `peertube-engine@*`. Today it hard-codes `peertube-engine.service` (line 72), which is silently empty after migration.
- New from this step: every writer of the snippet (the installer, the deploy's temp-file move, and the rollback's backup restore) leaves it mode 0644, so the updater can keep reading it.
</question>
<question id="4">
    Prod stops being one `peertube-engine.service` on 7070. It becomes one enabled instance of `peertube-engine@.service` on 7070 or 7071, reached only through `127.0.0.1:7079`, with the active port recorded only in `/etc/nginx/peertube-engine-upstream.conf`. The prod installers no longer accept an Engine host or port. A re-run without `--force` no longer restarts the Engine. The central installer still passes `--force` by default, so re-running it still restarts in place. `systemctl restart peertube-engine` and `journalctl -u peertube-engine` stop meaning anything in prod. The updater stops and starts whichever instance the snippet names, and it waits for, and is blocked by, the shared deploy lock. The Client's error body and log level during an Engine outage change as described in question 2. Dev is byte-for-byte unchanged in every touched file.
</question>

New impacts:
scripts/deploy-bluegreen.sh — snippet file mode after the step-7 temp-file move and after the rollback's backup restore. A `mktemp` temp file is root:root 0600, and a `mv` keeps that mode. nginx (root master) still loads it, but the prod updater runs as `User=${SERVICE_USER}` (engine/install-updater-service.sh:334) and reads the snippet through `--engine-upstream-snippet`. It gets `PermissionError`, so every nightly update fails at the snippet parse from the first deploy on. The failure comes before the stop, so it is silent to users, but the data stops updating. The snippet must be written 0644 (`chmod 0644` on the temp file before the `mv`, or `install -m 0644`). The same applies to the Engine installer's first write, under a restrictive sudo umask. The deploy test should assert the snippet's mode after a flip and after a rollback.

Inventory entries that did not hold up:
none

Conflicts: none

Recommendations: 1. **Snippet mode (new impact, take it).** Every snippet write leaves mode 0644: the installer's create, the deploy's temp file before the `mv`, and the rollback's restore. Add a mode assertion to `tests/active/test_deploy_bluegreen.py` and to the installer dry-run/contract test. Cost: about one line per writer and two assertions. Without it, the updater stops working after the first deploy.

2. **Refuse a target port that is already in use (closes the foreign-listener hole).** After stopping a leftover target instance (step 4) and before `systemctl start` (step 5), probe `127.0.0.1:<target>/api/health` once. If anything answers, refuse while still in `pre-switch`, having touched nothing. Also require `systemctl is-active` == `active` alongside the 200 in each readiness round. That costs nothing, because a `Type=simple` unit reports `active` from exec. Cost: about 10 lines of bash and one test case ("target port occupied → refused, nothing started"). This covers `server.py --dev` (default port 7071) and stray `run-services.sh` runs. Without it, a deploy can quietly hand production to a hand-started process and stop the real Engine. It is a refusal that changes no state, in the same class as the plan's two existing additions, so it fits the accepted tradeoffs. It still needs the operator's yes.

3. **Client 502 behaviour: keep the plan's "no Python change", and document it.** I checked every frontend data module: an HTML 502 degrades to the default message with no parse error. The only losses are the 0.25 s retry, the `ENGINE_PROXY_UNAVAILABLE` code, and the WARNING log line during Engine outages. Cost: a DEPLOYMENT.md note, already in the docs checklist. The alternative is about 10 lines in `_proxy_engine_request` and `_post_json` that treat a non-JSON 502/503/504 as a transport error, plus tests. Take it only if alerting keys on that code or log line.

4. **Give the 7079 listener its own `access_log`,** for example `/var/log/nginx/peertube-engine-internal.access.log`. Then the operator's "no 5xx spike in the public access log" check is not polluted by internal 502s during the updater's stop window. Cost: one line in the generated listener, plus one sentence in DEPLOYMENT §6.

5. **Write the four sudoers entries literally, and reject `--engine-service-name` in prod** in the updater installer, rather than deriving the entries from it. Cost: one guard. It removes the "silently ignored override" ambiguity the inventory flagged.

6. **Phase the engine and central installer changes together** (`--host`/`--port` rejection versus unconditional passing). In the same phase, update `watch-engine-logs.sh -prod` to `journalctl -u 'peertube-engine@*'`. Cost: none extra. It only constrains phase boundaries.

## 2026-09-30 - Step 3 - Identify every file, function and doc affected

Recorded ungated, at the operator direction.

### impacts


<impacts>
<impact path="scripts/deploy-bluegreen.sh" element="new script (the whole file)">
**What changes.** A new bash script that must run as root. It finds the repo root with the same `SCRIPT_DIR`/parent rule as `scripts/run-services.sh:24-29` and `scripts/install-service.sh:4-9`. It takes `--blue-green` (required), `--timeout` (default 300, same name as `run-services.sh:15,40,60`), `--warmup` (default 0), `--drain` (default 30), `--dry-run` and `-h`. The lock is `flock -n` on fd 9 of `<repo>/engine/server/db/engine-deploy.lock`. A phase variable (`pre-switch`, `switching`, `switched`) drives one rollback function, which the `INT`/`TERM` traps also call. Log lines are `deploy_id=… event=…` and go to stdout and to `logger -t peertube-engine-deploy`. The snippet path defaults to `/etc/nginx/peertube-engine-upstream.conf` and is overridable by one env var.

**What it depends on.**
- The snippet and the listener that `engine/install-engine-service.sh` writes, and the `peertube-engine@.service` template whose instance name is the port.
- Engine `/api/health` (`engine/server/api/handlers/similar.py:469-472`). It is rate-limited per `ip:path` before the health branch at 60 per 60 s (`engine/server/api/server_config.py:482-483`). `curl` sends no `X-Client-IP`, so every probe (readiness on `<target>`, the warm-up re-check, and the post-switch retries on 7079 that nginx forwards to the same instance) keys on `127.0.0.1:/api/health` in the new instance. At 2 s polls that is about 30 + 1 + 10 in a 60 s window: it fits, but with little margin. A 429 must count as "not ready".
- The temp-file contract of `random_cache_temp_path`/`remove_random_cache_temp` (`engine/server/data/random_cache.py:197-205`), which bash re-implements: `engine/server/db/random-cache.tmp.<MainPID>.db` plus the `-journal` sidecar.
- `peertube-updater.service` is `Type=oneshot` (`engine/install-updater-service.sh:333`), so `is-active` prints `activating` while it runs.
- For the Client preflight: `/etc/systemd/system/peertube-client.service`, whose `ExecStart` is written verbatim by `client/install-client-service.sh:197`.

**Risk of regression.**
- **Rollback correctness.** A wrong phase at the moment of failure either stops the only serving instance or leaves a snippet nginx has not loaded.
- **Snippet file mode.** If the new snippet is made with `mktemp` and moved into place, it is root `0600`. nginx (master runs as root) reads it fine, but the updater runs as the service user (`engine/install-updater-service.sh:334`) and can no longer parse it, so every updater run from the first deploy onward fails before its stop. The new file must be `chmod 0644` before the `mv`. The backup copy should keep the original mode as well.
- **Foreign listener.** A process already holding the target port gives a 200 while the unit sits in `activating (auto-restart)`. Examples: a manual `server.py --dev` (binds 7071 by default, `engine/server/api/server.py:141`), or `run-services.sh --engine-port 7071`. Readiness then passes on the wrong process, and only `failed`/`inactive` trip the immediate failure. The `X-Engine-Upstream` post-switch check would still name the target port, so it does not catch this either.
- **Lock after SIGKILL.** Short-lived children (`sleep` during the drain, `curl`, `logger`) inherit fd 9. A SIGKILL during the drain keeps the lock until that `sleep` exits. That is bounded, but "released on every exit" is not literally true unless children get `9>&-`.
- **Lock file ownership.** If root creates the lock file first, it is root-owned `0644` in the service user's directory (see the updater entry).
- **Preflight is an exact string match.** An equivalent URL (`http://localhost:7079`, a trailing `/`), a Client under a custom `--service-name`, or a `systemctl edit` drop-in overriding `ExecStart` is misjudged.
- **Backup file location.** The backup sits beside the snippet in `/etc/nginx/`, outside `conf.d/`, so nothing includes it. If it ever moved into `conf.d/` with a `.conf` suffix, nginx would load a duplicate `upstream`.
- **No precedent.** The script is new, so the cost of a bug lands on live traffic at the next deploy.
</impact>
<impact path="engine/install-engine-service.sh" element="install_engine_service() prod branch: unit path/content, --force block, enable/restart/verify, dry-run block, root/cmd requirements (lines 147-245)">
**What changes.**
- In prod, `unit_path` (line 170) becomes `/etc/systemd/system/peertube-engine@.service`, with `ExecStart=… --host 127.0.0.1 --port %i` (line 183). The rest of the content stays byte-identical. Dev keeps lines 170-244 as they are.
- New in prod, in order: take the deploy lock; write the template and listener; `daemon-reload`; migrate the legacy `peertube-engine.service` (stop, disable, `rm`, `daemon-reload`); read, create or validate the snippet; bring up the snippet's instance (start, restart only under `--force`, enable it and disable the other); then `nginx -t`, reload and a health check on 7079.

**Existing code that must change.**
- The `--force` block (lines 205-214) stops, disables, `rm`s and `reset-failed`s `${ENGINE_SERVICE_NAME}.service`. In prod that is the wrong unit.
- The enable, restart and verify lines (222-244) use `${ENGINE_SERVICE_NAME}.service` for `is-enabled`, `is-active`, `journalctl -u` and the Status/Logs hints. In prod they must use `peertube-engine@<port>`.
- The non-dry-run requirements (163-167) add `nginx`, `flock` and `curl` for prod. They use `$EUID`, unlike the deploy script's `id -u`.
- The dry-run block (191-202) must print previews of the template, snippet and listener, plus the migration and port plan, and must write nothing.

**What depends on it.**
- `scripts/install-service.sh:308-323,344`, through `engine_cmd`.
- `--print-default-service-name` (lines 311-315). `scripts/install-service.sh:147-155` and `updater-worker.py:38-79` both rely on it, so it must keep printing `peertube-engine`.
- `install_updater_with_timer` (126-145) passes `--engine-service-name ${ENGINE_SERVICE_NAME}`.
- The deploy script and the updater read the snippet this installer creates.

**Risk of regression.**
- **One-time migration outage.** The migration stops the live Engine.
- **Drop-ins lost.** `systemctl edit peertube-engine` drop-ins (`/etc/systemd/system/peertube-engine.service.d/`, which DEPLOYMENT.md §7 lines 447-448 tells operators to create for `RECOMMENDATIONS_DEBUG`) do not apply to `peertube-engine@.service` instances. The migration silently drops them. The installer should detect the directory and warn, or move it to `peertube-engine@.service.d/`. The same directory is left behind on uninstall.
- **Old updater unit after an Engine-only run.** If only this installer is run (not the central one), the old updater unit still runs `systemctl stop peertube-engine`, which no longer exists. The next updater run fails at the stop, before the merge. That fails safe but is broken until the updater installer is re-run. The docs or the installer must say so.
- **`--force` restarts in place.** The central installer passes `--force` for prod by default (`scripts/install-service.sh:270-273`), so every central re-run restarts the active instance in place, as today.
- **Invalid snippet.** It must fail before any stop.
- **nginx becomes mandatory.** A host without nginx, or with an `nginx.conf` that lacks the `conf.d` include, now fails the prod install where it used to succeed.
- **Dry-run reads `/etc/nginx`.** Reading the snippet for the dry-run port plan needs the same env override as the deploy script, or the pytest reads the real path.
- **Two lock paths.** The lock path comes from `PROJECT_DIR` after `realpath` (line 308), while the deploy derives it from its own location. A `--project-dir` that differs from the checkout gives two different locks.
- **`--service-name` in prod.** It is accepted today (line 261). If prod still honours it, the template name diverges from the `peertube-engine@` that the deploy, updater and sudoers hard-code. Reject it or ignore it, and decide which explicitly.
- **Snippet mode.** As in the deploy entry, the snippet must be written world-readable (`0644`) so the updater's service user can parse it.
</impact>
<impact path="engine/install-engine-service.sh" element="argument parsing (--host/--port lines 265-272), DEFAULT_PROD_ENGINE_PORT/resolve_default_engine_port (lines 23, 111-118), print_usage (lines 26-61)">

- The usage text, lines 35 (`prod: service=peertube-engine host=127.0.0.1 port=7070`) and 43-44 (`--host`, `--port … default: 7070 prod`), must describe the template, the 7070/7071 pair, the nginx files and the prod rejection.

**What depends on it.**
